subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 48-year-old woman with long-standing idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension undergoes lung biopsy at the time of transplantation. The pathologist examines the pulmonary arterioles. Which of the following vascular findings is most characteristic of her condition?
question: Which histologic finding is most consistent with long-standing pulmonary arterial hypertension?

options.text: Granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis
Diffuse alveolar flooding with hyaline membranes
Bronchial wall destruction with apical emphysematous bullae
Medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, and plexiform lesions of pulmonary arterioles
Neutrophilic alveolar infiltrates with pus and necrosis

explanation_correct: Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mm Hg at rest. Sustained elevation of pulmonary vascular resistance produces arteriosclerosis, medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, and the formation of plexiform lesions in the pulmonary arteries. These changes progressively raise right ventricular afterload, causing right ventricular hypertrophy and eventually right heart failure. The presence of plexiform lesions supports a diagnosis of severe, long-standing pulmonary arterial hypertension.

explanation_incorrect.A: Caseating granulomas are characteristic of tuberculosis or fungal infection, not the vascular remodeling of pulmonary hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.B: Diffuse alveolar hyaline membranes are the hallmark of ARDS, a permeability edema, not pulmonary arterial hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bronchial wall destruction with apical bullae describes emphysema; it is not the primary vascular lesion of pulmonary arterial hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neutrophilic infiltrates with pus indicate bacterial pneumonia, not the intimal and medial changes of pulmonary hypertension.

educationalObjective: Long-standing pulmonary hypertension causes medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, arteriosclerosis, and plexiform lesions in pulmonary arteries, leading to right ventricular pressure overload.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 30-year-old woman with a family history of pulmonary arterial hypertension undergoes genetic testing and is found to have a germline inactivating mutation in the BMPR2 gene. Her physicians discuss how this mutation leads to her disease.
question: Which of the following best explains the functional consequence of this mutation?

options.text: Loss of BMPR2 signaling removes inhibition of vascular smooth muscle proliferation, promoting pulmonary vascular remodeling
BMPR2 normally drives nitric oxide release, so its loss directly abolishes vasodilation
The mutation directly increases endothelin synthesis in pulmonary endothelial cells
It creates a congenital left-to-right shunt that increases pulmonary blood flow
It impairs surfactant production by type II pneumocytes, causing alveolar collapse

explanation_correct: BMPR2 encodes a receptor in the TGF-beta signaling pathway that normally inhibits vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation. An inactivating, loss-of-function mutation removes this restraint, allowing smooth muscle proliferation and pulmonary vascular remodeling that raise pulmonary vascular resistance. Heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension from BMPR2 mutations has a poor prognosis and a female predominance. This is distinct from the general endothelial dysfunction of pulmonary arterial hypertension, in which vasoconstrictors such as endothelin are increased and vasodilators such as nitric oxide and prostacyclin are decreased.

explanation_incorrect.B: The principal role of BMPR2 relevant here is inhibition of smooth muscle proliferation, not direct control of nitric oxide release.
explanation_incorrect.C: Increased endothelin is part of the broader endothelial dysfunction of PAH, not the direct consequence of a BMPR2 mutation.
explanation_incorrect.D: A left-to-right shunt is a congenital heart disease cause of pulmonary hypertension, not an effect of BMPR2 mutation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Surfactant production by type II pneumocytes is unrelated to BMPR2 signaling; that mechanism relates to neonatal and acute respiratory distress syndrome.

educationalObjective: BMPR2 normally inhibits vascular smooth muscle proliferation; inactivating mutations cause heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension with poor prognosis via unchecked vascular remodeling.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 64-year-old man with severe COPD and chronic hypoxemia is found to have an elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure on right heart catheterization. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular and valvular function, and he has no history of thromboembolism or connective tissue disease.
question: Into which World Health Organization group of pulmonary hypertension does his condition fall?

options.text: Group 1 — pulmonary arterial hypertension
Group 2 — left heart disease
Group 4 — chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
Group 5 — multifactorial and miscellaneous causes
Group 3 — lung disease and/or hypoxia

explanation_correct: Group 3 pulmonary hypertension results from underlying lung disease or chronic hypoxia, as occurs with COPD, interstitial lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea, or residence at high altitude. In COPD, destruction of the pulmonary vascular bed combined with hypoxic vasoconstriction raises pulmonary vascular resistance. This patient's severe COPD, hypoxemia, and normal left heart function place him squarely in group 3. Group 1 is pulmonary arterial hypertension, group 2 is left heart disease, group 4 is chronic thromboembolic disease, and group 5 covers multifactorial causes such as hematologic or metabolic disorders and tumor compression.

explanation_incorrect.A: Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension includes idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced, and connective-tissue-disease-associated cases, not hypertension secondary to COPD.
explanation_incorrect.B: Group 2 is due to left heart disease such as systolic or diastolic dysfunction and valvular disease, which are absent here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Group 4 results from recurrent microthrombi reducing the pulmonary vascular bed; there is no thromboembolic history in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.D: Group 5 encompasses hematologic, systemic, and metabolic disorders or tumor compression, which does not describe uncomplicated COPD.

educationalObjective: Hypoxemic lung diseases such as COPD, interstitial lung disease, and sleep apnea cause group 3 pulmonary hypertension via hypoxic vasoconstriction and loss of vascular bed.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing pulmonary hypertension has a palpable Parasternal heave along the left sternal border on physical examination. She also has elevated neck veins and peripheral edema.
question: Which of the following best explains the cause of the parasternal heave?

options.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy from long-standing systemic hypertension
Right ventricular hypertrophy from increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular pressure overload
Isolated right atrial enlargement from tricuspid regurgitation
A large pericardial effusion muffling the heart sounds
Pulmonary edema secondary to left-sided heart failure

explanation_correct: In pulmonary hypertension, increased pulmonary vascular resistance raises right ventricular pressure and afterload. The right ventricle responds with hypertrophy, and the hypertrophied chamber generates a palpable parasternal heave along the left sternal border. Progressive pressure overload can evolve into right heart failure with jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema, as seen in this patient. Recognizing the heave therefore points to underlying right ventricular pressure overload from the pulmonary hypertension.

explanation_incorrect.A: Left ventricular hypertrophy produces a displaced, forceful apical impulse rather than a parasternal heave and results from systemic, not pulmonary, hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.C: Right atrial enlargement does not generate the systolic parasternal lift; the heave reflects right ventricular hypertrophy.
explanation_incorrect.D: A pericardial effusion causes muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus, not a parasternal heave.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pulmonary edema from left heart failure belongs to group 2 physiology and does not produce a right ventricular heave.

educationalObjective: A parasternal heave in pulmonary hypertension reflects right ventricular hypertrophy from increased pulmonary vascular resistance and RV pressure overload, which can progress to right heart failure.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 60-year-old patient has decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right upper lung field. Tactile fremitus is decreased over the same area, and the trachea is deviated toward the right side.
question: Which of the following conditions is most consistent with these findings?

options.text: Atelectasis
Large pleural effusion
Simple pneumothorax
Tension pneumothorax
Lobar consolidation

explanation_correct: Atelectasis is alveolar collapse that reduces the volume of the affected lung, producing decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and decreased tactile fremitus. Because the affected lung shrinks, mediastinal structures and the trachea are pulled toward the side of the lesion. This distinguishes atelectasis from a large pleural effusion or tension pneumothorax, in which the trachea is pushed away from the lesion. The combination of decreased sounds, dullness, and tracheal deviation toward the lesion is classic for atelectasis.

explanation_incorrect.B: A large pleural effusion also causes dullness and decreased breath sounds and fremitus, but it pushes the trachea away from the lesion rather than toward it.
explanation_incorrect.C: Simple pneumothorax produces hyperresonance to percussion and no tracheal deviation, not dullness with deviation toward the lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tension pneumothorax produces hyperresonance and deviates the trachea away from the affected side, often with hypotension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Consolidation causes bronchial breath sounds, increased fremitus, and egophony, with no tracheal deviation.

educationalObjective: Atelectasis causes decreased breath sounds, dullness, and decreased fremitus with tracheal deviation toward the lesion because the affected lung loses volume.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 24-year-old man with fever and a productive cough is diagnosed with lobar pneumonia. On examination of the affected lobe, the clinician notes abnormal sounds and percussion findings. Which set of findings is most likely over the consolidated region?
question: Which of the following examination findings is most characteristic of consolidation?

options.text: Decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance, and decreased fremitus
Decreased breath sounds, dullness, and tracheal deviation toward the lesion
Decreased breath sounds, dullness, and tracheal deviation away from the lesion
Bronchial breath sounds, late inspiratory crackles, egophony, dullness, and increased fremitus
Hyperresonance, decreased fremitus, and tracheal deviation away from the lesion

explanation_correct: Consolidation, as in lobar pneumonia or pulmonary edema, fills alveoli with fluid and inflammatory material, which transmits sound and vibrations better than aerated lung. This produces bronchial breath sounds, late inspiratory crackles, egophony, and whispered pectoriloquy, along with dullness to percussion and increased tactile fremitus. Lung volume is preserved, so there is no significant tracheal deviation. These findings contrast with effusion and pneumothorax, in which breath sounds and fremitus are decreased.

explanation_incorrect.A: Decreased breath sounds with hyperresonance and decreased fremitus describes a simple pneumothorax, not consolidation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Decreased sounds, dullness, and tracheal deviation toward the lesion describes atelectasis with volume loss.
explanation_incorrect.C: Decreased sounds, dullness, and tracheal deviation away from the lesion describes a large pleural effusion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hyperresonance with decreased fremitus and tracheal deviation away describes a tension pneumothorax.

educationalObjective: Consolidation produces bronchial breath sounds, late inspiratory crackles, egophony, dullness, and increased fremitus without tracheal deviation because lung volume is maintained.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 28-year-old tall, thin man presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Examination shows decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance, and decreased fremitus over the right hemithorax. His trachea is midline and his blood pressure is normal. He is diagnosed with a spontaneous pneumothorax.
question: Which of the following statements best distinguishes his likely condition from the more dangerous tension pneumothorax?

options.text: Tension pneumothorax produces hyperresonance with tracheal deviation toward the affected side
Tension pneumothorax typically shows hyperresonance with a midline trachea and normal blood pressure
Simple pneumothorax produces dullness to percussion with tracheal deviation away from the lesion
Simple pneumothorax produces dullness with tracheal deviation toward the lesion
Simple pneumothorax shows hyperresonance without tracheal deviation, whereas tension pneumothorax deviates the trachea away and can cause hypotension

explanation_correct: This patient has a simple primary spontaneous pneumothorax: air in the pleural space causes hyperresonance, decreased breath sounds, and decreased fremitus without mediastinal shift. In tension pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space but cannot exit, so pressure builds, the trachea deviates away from the affected side, the IVC is kinked, venous return falls, and hypotension develops. His midline trachea and normal blood pressure indicate a simple rather than tension mechanism. Because tension pneumothorax can rapidly be fatal, it requires immediate needle decompression.

explanation_incorrect.A: In tension pneumothorax the trachea deviates away from the affected side, not toward it.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tension pneumothorax causes tracheal deviation away from the lesion and often hypotension, not a midline trachea with normal pressure.
explanation_incorrect.C: Simple pneumothorax produces hyperresonance, not dullness, and does not deviate the trachea.
explanation_incorrect.D: Dullness with tracheal deviation toward the lesion describes atelectasis, not pneumothorax.

educationalObjective: Simple pneumothorax causes hyperresonance and decreased breath sounds without tracheal deviation; tension pneumothorax adds tracheal deviation away, reduced venous return, and hypotension requiring emergency decompression.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Pulmonary hypertension and physical findings in lung disease
vignette: A 62-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has broadening of his fingertips and loss of the normal angle between the nail bed and nail plate. His physician recognizes this as digital clubbing.
question: Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this finding?

options.text: Chronic hypoxemia directly causing resorption of distal phalangeal bone
Deposition of immune complexes within the nail bed connective tissue
Platelets and megakaryocytes lodged in digital vasculature releasing PDGF and VEGF
Vitamin D excess from macrophage activation causing bony overgrowth
Reflex sympathetic vasoconstriction of the digital arteries

explanation_correct: Digital clubbing is defined by an increased angle greater than 180 degrees between the nail bed and the nail plate. In patients with intrapulmonary shunting, platelets and megakaryocytes bypass the pulmonary circulation and become lodged in the digital vasculature, where they release platelet-derived growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor. These mediators promote connective tissue and bone growth in the fingertips. Causes include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, lung cancer, cyanotic congenital heart disease, lung abscess, tuberculosis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Notably, clubbing is not typically associated with COPD or asthma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Clubbing is not simply a direct effect of hypoxemia on bone; it is mediated by platelet and megakaryocyte-derived growth factors.
explanation_incorrect.B: Immune complex deposition is not the mechanism; the driving factors are PDGF and VEGF released in the digital circulation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Macrophage-derived vitamin D in granulomatous disease is associated with hypercalcemia, not the local digital changes of clubbing.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sympathetic vasoconstriction would reduce digital blood flow and does not produce the proliferative changes of clubbing.

educationalObjective: Digital clubbing results from platelets and megakaryocytes lodging in digital vessels and releasing PDGF and VEGF; it is seen with IPF, CF, bronchiectasis, lung cancer, cyanotic heart disease, and IBD but not typically COPD or asthma.
